Tel-abib
TEL-uh-BEEB
proper noun
Hebrew Tel Aviv, “mound of the ear of corn” or “hill of the flood”; the settlement of the Judean captives by the river Chebar where Ezekiel dwelt among them.

📖 Biblical Definition

Tel-abib was a settlement of the exiles by the river Chebar, one of the mounds of Babylon where the carried-away of Judah were planted far from Zion. It is named in a single unforgettable verse, when the prophet returned from the vision of the glory of God to sit among his afflicted people: “Then I came to them of the captivity at Telabib, that dwelt by the river of Chebar, and I sat where they sat, and remained there astonished among them seven days” (Eze 3:15). Here is the tenderness of the prophetic office and, deeper still, a figure of the gospel. Ezekiel did not preach at a distance to the exiles; he came to them, dwelt where they dwelt, and sat where they sat, silent and overwhelmed for seven days, bearing in his own soul the weight of their captivity before ever he opened his mouth. The LORD would not leave His people comfortless in the strange land; He set His prophet in the midst of them, and His presence went with them into exile. So the greater Prophet came not to a throne but to a manger, and sat where we sit, taking our flesh, bearing our burden, entering our estrangement under the curse. The God who placed Ezekiel at Tel-abib is the God who is with His people in every Babylon, and who will bring them home.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The settlement of the captives by the river Chebar where Ezekiel sat astonished among them (Eze 3:15); a witness to the LORD’s presence with His people in exile and a figure of the Prophet who sits where His people sit.

TEL-ABIB, a settlement of the exiles by the river Chebar.

One of the mounds of Babylon where captive Judah was planted.

There Ezekiel came to the captivity and sat where they sat (Eze 3:15).

He remained astonished among them seven days, bearing their burden.

A figure of the greater Prophet who comes to His people in their exile.

📖 Key Scripture

Eze 3:15 — "Then I came to them of the captivity at Telabib, that dwelt by the river of Chebar, and I sat where they sat, and remained there astonished among them seven days."

Isa 43:3 — "For I am the LORD thy God, the Holy One of Israel, thy Saviour: I gave Egypt for thy ransom, Ethiopia and Seba for thee."

Isa 11:11 — "And it shall come to pass in that day, that the Lord shall set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant of his people, which shall be left, from Assyria, and from Egypt, and from Pathros, and from Cush, and from Elam, and from Shinar, and from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea."

Act 17:26 — "And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation;"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The exile settlement by the Chebar where Ezekiel sat among the captives; the entry recovers the LORD’s presence with His people in their affliction and the Prophet who bears their burden.

expand to see more

Tel-abib is a mound in Babylon known for one thing — a prophet sitting silent among the captives — and it stirs no modern quarrel. Its lesson is nearness: the LORD did not leave His exiles comfortless, but set His prophet in their midst.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the presence of God with His afflicted people. Ezekiel came to them, sat where they sat, and was astonished seven days before he spoke, bearing their suffering in his own soul. So the greater Prophet took our flesh and sat where we sit under the curse; and the God who placed Ezekiel at Tel-abib will recover the remnant of His people and bring them home.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Tel Aviv, “mound of corn-ears” or “hill of the flood”; a place-name of the Chaldean plain where the captives dwelt.

expand to see more

Tel-abib — Hebrew Tel Aviv, a mound or ruin-heap of Babylon.

Tel is a mound of ruins; abib, the green ear of corn or the flood.

A settlement of the captivity by the river Chebar (Eze 3:15).

The Chebar was a canal of the Babylonian plain, place of Ezekiel’s visions.

There the prophet sat where the exiles sat, astonished seven days.

Usage

"Ezekiel came to the captivity at Tel-abib by the river Chebar."

"He sat where they sat and remained astonished seven days."

"Tel-abib witnesses the LORD’s presence with His people in exile."
